I've been farming here in Quzhou for over forty years. At my age, I don't gamble with new crops or fancy techniques. This land is good for two things: winter wheat and summer maize. That's the rotation my father did, and that's what I'll stick with. I've got 15 mu — not a big farm, but enough for me and my wife to manage without hiring too much help.

My wheat went in last October, and now it's greening up. I'll topdress it with urea when the weather warms — the crop needs a good feed at green-up and again at jointing. I buy improved wheat seeds from the supply shop in town; they're not the most expensive ones, but they give steady yields. For the maize that follows the wheat in June, I'll plant a hybrid variety — everyone here uses hybrids now, you can't match the yield with open-pollinated seed.

I use the rotary tiller. It's quick and doesn't cost as much as deep ploughing. Between wheat harvest and maize sowing, I only have a few days, so I need something fast. I irrigate my wheat four times if the rain is short — winter irrigation if it's dry, then green-up water, jointing water, and one more at heading. The maize I'll irrigate twice, at sowing and when it's at the big trumpet stage. I spray herbicide in spring for the wheat, and fungicide at heading. For maize, herbicide at sowing and insecticide once for corn borers. I don't cut corners on fertilizer — I put down compound fertilizer as basal and top up with urea. The land here needs feeding to produce.

I don't grow cotton anymore — too much labor picking it, and my back isn't what it used to be. Vegetables? Too risky. The price jumps around, and you need constant spraying and watering. Grain prices are stable, the government gives a small subsidy, and the dealer comes to the village to buy it. That's good enough for me.
